mappings.note: Narrates Alexander's Indian campaign, the defeat of Porus and the forced retreat. Event history; no administrative or military measure of a state is analysed.
The Gymnosophists episode as a meeting of Greek power and Indian philosophical traditions - cultural contact. Not LO-81, because no religious movement arises from it.
Kautilya's role as strategist and political guide in building the Mauryan state. Statecraft, so LO-78 rather than a biographical recall.
The Arthashastra's subject matter - politics, governance, law, defence, administration. Not CG-SST2, because the answer is about statecraft content, not about the text as a dated source.
Sets out all seven limbs of the kingdom. The anatomy of a governed state, so LO-78.
Kautilya's principle that the king's welfare lies in his subjects' welfare is a doctrine of governance. Not CG-SST2.
Who Megasthenes was and why Indika matters as an early foreign, partly lost, second-hand account. Directly the 'how historians study the past using different types of sources' clause.
The Kalinga war as the event that changed Ashoka's life and policies. A ruler's policy turn, so LO-78; the item on whose teachings guided that turn carries LO-81 instead.
Edicts as official declarations used to broadcast policy and Dhamma to subjects - an instrument of governance. Not CG-SST2, because their purpose, not their value as evidence, is asked.
Prakrit and Brahmi as the language and script of the edicts, with Brahmi noted as the ancestor of later scripts. A fact about the sources themselves.
Dhamma as the moral code Ashoka promoted across his empire - the ideology of his rule. Not LO-81, which is kept for Buddhism as a movement.
Medical care, rest houses, wells and tree planting are Ashoka's public works. Administration and welfare, not religious doctrine.
Describes Pataliputra's palaces, streets and wooden houses - urban life in the period. Not LO-78, because the city is described rather than its administration analysed.
The Sohagaura plate as evidence of state granaries and famine preparedness. The question asks what it says about administration, so LO-78 despite the inscription being a source.
Cotton garments and leather shoes of the period - everyday social history from later accounts. No LO covers material culture.
What the polished pillars and Sarnath capital signify about craftsmanship and imperial symbolism. Not LO-80, because a free-standing pillar is not a temple, tomb or mosque; this is art as evidence.
Two reasons empires fall - resentful tributaries, weak successors, breakaway regions, economic crisis. Reasoning about the limits of imperial control.
Ambition, resources, trade-route revenue and military power as motives for expansion. State-building strategy, so LO-78.
Guilds fostering economic stability and social self-organisation, explicitly with reduced state interference. Economic and social history; LO-78 would wrongly make them organs of the state.
Soil, iron ore, forests and rivers as the base for Magadha's rise - economic geography. Not LO-78, because the answer stops at advantages rather than describing governance.

Sets Mahapadma Nanda's expansion and unpopularity against Chandragupta's conquests and Kautilyan administration - a direct comparison of two rulers, which is exactly LO-79. The single-ruler items carry LO-78.
Weighs the limited political against the lasting cultural effects of Alexander's invasion, including Indo-Greek contact. A judgement about historical development, not about administration.
Tests the Arthashastra's pragmatism through armies, spies, taxes, justice and diplomacy - the practical machinery of rule. Statecraft throughout, so LO-78.
Analyses why all seven limbs are interdependent for a strong kingdom. The fullest saptanga item, squarely administration.

The political dimension - consolidating a vast empire by welfare and diplomacy - is LO-78, while the ethical dimension rests on Ashoka's embrace of Buddhist non-violence, which is LO-81. The question asks for both, so both are cited.
Evaluates the edicts as a governing tool for reaching a diverse empire - placement, language, permanence. Administration, so LO-78 rather than the sources goal.
Dhamma weighed as genuine moral conviction after Kalinga (LO-81, the reach of Buddhist ideas) and as a unifying ideology serving imperial control (LO-78). Neither code alone carries the statement.

Asks about Mauryan art and architecture through the Sarnath capital and the Great Stupa at Sanchi, including stone technique. LO-80 is the frame's only architecture outcome, and the stupa is the nearest thing in it to a relic monument.

The question names Megasthenes' account and the Sohagaura plate as the evidence (CG-SST2) and asks what they reveal about state support for agriculture and food security (LO-78). Both halves are explicit in the stem.
Distance, breakaway governors, weak successors and fiscal strain as the fragilities of empire. Reasoning about imperial control, the same lane as the other decline items.
Political unity securing trade routes, standardising coinage and keeping order for commerce is administration serving the economy. Not CG-SST2, because the state's action is the subject.
Tests whether subject welfare is idealism or sound policy - contented subjects rebel less, produce more and pay more tax. A judgement about governance.

A satrap losing his grip after Alexander's death, with restless chiefs, disrupted revenue and a rival power rising - all about holding or losing control of territory. Not CG-SST2, because each part reasons about authority.

Parts (i) and (ii) are about how a guild organises standards and protects caravans (CG-SST2, economic self-organisation), while part (iii) asks whether the ruler would interfere with guild rules, which is a question about state authority (LO-78).

An inspecting officer applying Ashoka's instructions on impartiality and officials' conduct is the enforcement of imperial policy. Not LO-81: tolerance of sects appears as a rule of administration, not as a religious movement.
Seals, storage jars and an Arthashastra fragment have to be read as evidence (CG-SST2), and what they reveal is a revenue and garrison outpost on a trade route (LO-78). The item works at both levels.

A Deccan tributary refusing tribute after Ashoka's death, and the consequences for both sides, is about the mechanics of imperial control and its failure. Not CG-SST2, because every part reasons about authority and revenue.
